segments.en: That wild cackle in the gum trees at sunrise is a kookaburra, laughing the day awake. In Australia, even the birds seem to have a sense of humour, and plenty of the people do too.
Australia is both a country and a whole continent, an island so big that it holds tropical rainforest, snowy mountains, vast deserts and long, golden beaches, all under one sky.

Long before anyone else arrived, this land was home to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, whose cultures are among the oldest living cultures on Earth. Their stories and art connect every rock, river and waterhole to the land itself.
In the red heart of the country stands Uluru, a huge sandstone rock sacred to its Anangu custodians. At sunset it glows orange, then deep red, then purple, as though it were lit from within.
Most Australians live near the coast. Children learn to swim early, and on busy beaches volunteer lifesavers in red and yellow caps keep watch between the flags.

Off the northeast coast lies the Great Barrier Reef, a living wonder of coral stretching for thousands of kilometres. Snorkel over it and you might meet turtles, clownfish and rays gliding past like shadows.

And then there are the animals you will not find anywhere else in the wild: kangaroos bounding across the plains, sleepy koalas in eucalyptus trees, wombats, echidnas and the odd, duck-billed platypus.
Sydney wraps around a sparkling harbour, where the white sails of the Opera House face the great arch of the Harbour Bridge. Melbourne is known for its laneways, coffee and street art.
Australians love a relaxed greeting. A cheerful g'day works almost anywhere, and words get friendly nicknames, so an afternoon becomes an arvo and a barbecue becomes a barbie.

And barbecues are everywhere, in gardens, parks and on beaches, often on free public grills. A grilled sausage in a slice of bread is a classic. For breakfast, try toast with Vegemite, spread very thinly.
Sport is a national passion. Summer means cricket, winter means football, and in the southern states that usually means Australian rules, a fast, high-flying game played on a huge oval field.
People here value a fair go and looking out for your mates. Offer to help, bring something to share when you are invited, and you will fit right in.
When you are ready, fly east across the Tasman Sea, where New Zealand is waiting with green hills, fiery volcanoes and a warm kia ora.
